2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Serious concern: Severe missing data across Brazil's ~5,570 municipalities over 2013-2020 reduced the analytic sample to 1,157 observations (1,159 in Table 2), driven by scarce administrative reporting on transaction-cost/investment variables and logarithmic exclusion of zero-investment municipality-years; state-stratified bootstrapping only resampled observed cases without addressing missing-data bias.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious concern: Municipalities self-select into regional consortia via city council vote largely due to fiscal distress and low baseline sewage coverage (acknowledged as a driver of cooperation on p. 6), creating reverse causality/confounding by indication; no quasi-experimental design is used, key municipal fiscal/economic confounders are omitted, between-subjects SPSS GLM (11 df) does not absorb municipality fixed effects, and contemporaneous water/sewage investments (post-treatment mediators) are conditioned on.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate to weak: Although Section 2.3 describes Brazil's constitutional decentralization, 2007 federal sanitation guidelines, programmatic contracts, city council voting rules, and 2020 Sanitation Legal Framework Act, the empirical model collapses institutional participation into a binary consortium dummy (1/0) and proxies contract management complexity only by water-only vs. combined water-and-wastewater scope, while Table 1 (contractual tools) is blank in the published PDF.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Consortium participation, investments, and coverage rely on national administrative/survey databases (IBGE MUNIC, FINBRA, SNIS), but consortium exposure lacks entry/exit timing and contract-type granularity, self-reported municipal accounting/SNIS data vary in accuracy across small vs. large municipalities, and text descriptions mix log-transformed and raw scales.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Outcomes (municipal total sanitation expenditure and indices of total population served by water and sewage services) derive from standardized official national sources (FINBRA, IBGE, SNIS), but measure only aggregate spending and nominal population coverage without service continuity, water quality, or actual wastewater treatment performance, and Section 4 inconsistently reports log and unlogged group means.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol was registered, and multiple internal reporting inconsistencies appear (Table 1 has no content; sample size is 1,159 in Table 2 vs. 1,157 in Table 3; Density is omitted from Table 4 without explanation due to exact log-collinearity with Population and Area; Section 5 claims service coverage improved under cooperative agreements despite negative/lower sewage coverage estimates for cooperation in Section 4 and Tables 3-4).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Serious concern: Inclusion in the 1,157-observation panel required matched non-missing positive water and sewage investment records (log-transformed) from SNIS/FINBRA/IBGE, selecting a small, non-random fraction of municipality-years without defining incident consortium entry vs. prevalent membership or comparing included and excluded municipalities.

domain_ratings.justification: Municipalities voluntarily enter regional consortia via city council vote (p. 3), and the authors explicitly note on p. 6 that low baseline sewage coverage and fiscal constraints drive municipalities to join consortia (confounding by indication / reverse causality). No quasi-experimental identification strategy (e.g., DiD with staggered entry, IV, or matching) is used. Although p. 5 refers to 'a multivariate general linear model with fixed effects', the estimation tests 'between-subject effects' in SPSS with only 11 model degrees of freedom (Table 3), meaning municipality fixed effects were not absorbed. Critical time-varying and baseline confounders (municipal tax revenue, federal transfers, GDP per capita, baseline infrastructure) are omitted, and the model conditions on contemporaneous water and sewage capital investments, which are post-intervention mediators/components of total expenditure.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 3] Section 2.3; [PDF Pages 4-5] Section 3; [PDF Pages 5-6] Section 4, Tables 3-4

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Across roughly 5,570 Brazilian municipalities over 8 years (2013-2020), only 1,159 observations in Table 2 (1,157 in Table 3) enter the analysis because selection required complete matched records including positive water and sewage investments (log-transformed). Selection into the analytic sample thus depends on post-intervention capital investment reporting, the number of unique municipalities is unreported, and prevalent vs. new consortium entrants during 2013-2020 are not distinguished.

Participation in regional sanitation consortia is coded from official records (IBGE MUNIC, FINBRA, SNIS) as a binary indicator (1 = engaged in consortia, 0 = not engaged). However, the paper does not specify whether consortium status was tracked annually or taken from cross-sectional IBGE MUNIC 2020 data, does not distinguish planning/regulatory consortia from full service-delivery program contracts, does not track entry or exit dates ('cooperative units are free to leave consortia if they desire', p. 3), and leaves Table 1 ('Contractual tools and expected transaction costs for sanitation services in Brazil') completely blank on p. 4.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: The study evaluates routine institutional participation in consortia, but notes that cooperating municipalities may fail to fulfill agreed programmatic investments (facing penalties or voluntary exit, p. 3) and does not account for concurrent delegation to state water companies or private concessions. Moreover, adjusting for contemporaneous water and sewage investment variables blocks/distorts part of the intended capital-investment pathway of consortium participation.

The authors explicitly state that scarce transaction-cost/investment data reduced the 2013-2020 national municipal panel to 1,157 observations (p. 4), and taking logarithms of water and sewage investment further excludes any municipality-year with zero investment. Complete-case analysis is performed without diagnostics comparing included and excluded municipalities; state-stratified bootstrapping (1,000 resamples) only reweights/resamples within the observed 1,157 complete records and cannot correct non-random missingness across unrecorded municipalities.

Total sanitation expenditure and water/sewage population-served indices come from standardized national administrative systems (FINBRA, SNIS, IBGE) rather than subjective investigator assessment. Nonetheless, self-reported municipal accounting and SNIS utility indicators are subject to administrative reporting error correlated with municipal institutional capacity, and the manuscript exhibits scale-reporting inconsistencies in Section 4 (mixing log-transformed means such as M = 6.1 with apparent raw percentage/log figures such as M = 52.0 and M = 10.90).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan or protocol exists to verify pre-specified model structure or outcome/interaction definitions. In addition, there are visible reporting inconsistencies across tables and text: Table 1 is blank; sample size shifts between 1,159 (Table 2) and 1,157 (Table 3); log population density is included in Table 3 despite exact collinearity with log population and log area and then silently dropped in Table 4; and Section 5 asserts that service coverage improved under cooperative agreements whereas Section 4 and Tables 3-4 show lower sewage coverage under cooperation.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Silvestre et al. (2022) conduct a comparative panel analysis (2013-2020; N = 1,157 municipality-year observations from IBGE, FINBRA, and SNIS) evaluating the relationship between municipal participation in formal regional sanitation consortia (vs. stand-alone non-cooperation) and municipal sanitation expenditure, water service coverage, and sewage service coverage in Brazil. Appraised with ROBINS-I as a non-randomized comparative panel evaluation of an institutional governance arrangement, the study is at Serious overall risk of bias. Three domains are rated Serious: (1) confounding (D1), because municipalities self-select into consortia via city council vote specifically in response to low baseline coverage and fiscal stress, no quasi-experimental identification strategy is employed, municipality fixed effects are not absorbed in the 11-df between-subjects SPSS GLM despite 'fixed effects' terminology, key fiscal/socioeconomic confounders are omitted, and contemporaneous water/sewage investments (post-treatment mediators) are conditioned on; (2) participant selection (D2) and (3) missing data (D5), because restricting to matched, log-transformed positive water and sewage investment observations collapses roughly 5,570 Brazilian municipalities over eight years to just 1,157 complete observations without diagnostics on excluded municipalities or distinction between incident and prevalent consortium members. Classification of interventions (D3), deviations from intended interventions (D4), measurement of outcomes (D6), and selection of the reported result (D7—no pre-registration plus internal table/text inconsistencies including a blank Table 1 and contradictory coverage conclusions in Section 5) are each rated Moderate risk of bias.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal panel observational study (2013-2020 unbalanced panel of 1,157 Brazilian municipality-year observations comparing consortia-participating vs. non-cooperating municipalities using multivariate general linear model regression with state-stratified bootstrapping)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Institutional background in Section 2.3 ([PDF Pages 3-4]); data sources, variable definitions, sample size (N = 1,157 / 1,159), and SPSS GLM / bootstrap empirical strategy in Section 3 and Tables 1-2 ([PDF Pages 4-5]); regression and parameter estimates in Section 4 and Tables 3-4 ([PDF Pages 5-6]); conclusions and limitations in Section 5 ([PDF Pages 6-7]).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the appropriate instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study is a non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation of a formal public policy/institutional governance intervention (municipal entry into regional sanitation consortia via programmatic contract vs. a comparator group of stand-alone non-cooperating municipalities) estimating effects on municipal sanitation expenditure and water/wastewater population coverage over 2013-2020.
